fullDescription:
A night on Bai Tu Long, the bay that licensing keeps quiet.

There are three bays in this UNESCO landscape and they are one continuous drowned karst divided by administration, not geology. Ha Long proper carries almost the whole cruise fleet. Bai Tu Long runs northeast towards the Chinese border, and the number of boats permitted to work it is capped, so it stays genuinely empty in a way Ha Long has not been for twenty years.

The name is part of a pair. Ha Long means descending dragon, the mother sent down to defend Vietnam whose spat jade became the islands. Bai Tu Long is where her children came down after her.

Thien Canh Son cave sits on a small island reached by a short climb, and it is the reason the route goes this way: stalactite chambers that receive a handful of boats a day rather than the queue that forms at Sung Sot in the main bay.

Vung Vieng is a floating fishing village, families living on rafts with fish pens beneath them, worked by rowing boat rather than engine so the visit stays quiet.

Kayaking happens off the boat in sheltered water between the karsts, which is how you get into the low openings a cruise hull cannot enter.

The overnight is what makes it. Day boats leave in the late afternoon and return after dawn, and Bai Tu Long starts emptier than Ha Long to begin with.

We book with DGB Travel directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers an English guide on the cruise, a welcome cocktail, all Ha Long Bay entrance and sightseeing fees, and your accommodation on board.

Two days, one night. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Bai Tu Long, where licensing caps the number of boats
Named for the dragon children, after Ha Long's mother dragon
Thien Canh Son cave, a handful of boats a day rather than a queue
Vung Vieng floating village, worked by rowing boat
Entrance and sightseeing fees included, not charged aboard

fullDescription:
Three and a half hours making a stained glass piece in Saigon, and you take it home finished.

The method is copper foil, the Tiffany technique, rather than the lead came used in cathedral windows. Each piece of glass is scored, broken along the score, ground smooth on a wet wheel, wrapped in adhesive copper tape and then soldered to its neighbours. That sequence is why a small panel takes three and a half hours: the cutting is quick and the grinding and foiling are not.

Cutting glass is the part people expect to be frightening and find is not. You are not cutting through it, you are scoring a line and then using the break to run along that line, which is closer to snapping a bar of chocolate than to sawing.

The soldering is where it becomes a thing rather than pieces. Molten solder pulled along a foil seam beads into a raised line, and how smooth that bead runs is what separates a first piece from a tenth.

No experience is assumed, all tools and materials are provided, and the instructor works in English throughout.

It is indoor and air-conditioned, which in Saigon matters for three and a half hours in the middle of the day, and it runs regardless of the wet-season afternoons between May and November.

We book with Viva Vietnam directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers the English-speaking instructor, all tools and materials, and your finished piece to take home.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Copper foil method, the one Tiffany used, not cathedral lead
Score and snap rather than saw: easier than it sounds
Grinding and foiling are what take the time, not the cutting
Solder beaded along the seam turns pieces into a panel
Indoors and air-conditioned, reliable through the wet season

fullDescription:
Ninety minutes blending a perfume in Saigon, and you leave with a bottle of it.

The session starts with fragrance families, which is the vocabulary that makes the rest make sense: floral, citrus, woody, oriental, fougère. Once you can place a scent in a family you can predict what it will sit well beside, and that is most of what a perfumer does.

Then layering. A perfume is built in three tiers. Top notes are the citrus and herbs that arrive first and are gone within minutes. Heart notes, the florals and spices, hold the middle hours. Base notes are the woods, resins and vanillas still on your skin in the evening, and they are why one scent lasts and another disappears by lunch.

You test on blotters before you commit, because the nose stops registering a smell after a few minutes and the order you sample in changes what you pick.

Vietnam supplies a good deal of what goes into this: cinnamon from Quang Nam, star anise from the north, and agarwood, the resin behind oud and one of the most expensive materials in perfumery.

You take home one bottle of your own formula, written down so it can be made again.

Indoors and short, so it works as an afternoon in the heat or when the rain sets in.

We book with Viva Vietnam directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers the introduction to fragrance families and layering, all materials and ingredients, and one take-home bottle of your perfume.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Fragrance families first, so the blending makes sense
Three tiers: top notes go in minutes, base notes last all day
Blotters before committing, because the nose tires fast
Vietnamese cinnamon, star anise and agarwood among the oils
One bottle to take home, with the formula written down

fullDescription:
Two hours of Hmong batik in Sapa: draw in wax, dye in indigo, take the cloth home.

The technique is wax resist. Molten beeswax is drawn onto hemp cloth with a chan, a small copper-tipped pen that holds the wax hot enough to flow, and the cloth then goes into an indigo vat. The dye takes everywhere the wax is not, so when the wax is boiled out your drawing appears white against blue.

The indigo is the part that surprises people. The vat is a living fermentation, fed and kept warm over weeks rather than mixed on the day, and cloth comes out of it green and turns blue in front of you as it meets the air.

Hmong patterns are not decoration. Spirals, snail shells, elephant feet and ram's horns each carry meaning, and women learn them from their mothers rather than from a book. The instructor will tell you what you are drawing before you draw it.

No experience is expected. Two hours is enough for a small piece done properly.

You take home the textile you made.

This runs whatever the weather, which in Sapa is worth more than it sounds. Cloud fills the valley for much of the year and closes the views and the paragliding; nothing here depends on seeing the mountains.

We book with Ethnic Community Cultural Tours directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers the hands-on workshop, instructor guidance, beeswax painting materials, the natural indigo dyeing and your handmade textile.

Two hours. Wear something you do not mind marking. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Wax resist drawn with the traditional copper-tipped chan
A living indigo vat: cloth comes out green, turns blue in the air
Patterns carry meaning, learned mother to daughter
No experience needed, and the textile is yours
Runs when cloud closes Sapa's views and flights

fullDescription:
Two hours cooking two Vietnamese dishes in Ta Van, in the valley below Sapa.

Ta Van sits in the Muong Hoa valley among the rice terraces, a Giay and Hmong village along the river, and the class happens there with a local host rather than in a Sapa town kitchen. Getting down into the valley is part of it: the terraces look completely different from below than they do from the ridge.

Two dishes done properly beats six done badly, which is the shape of this class. You cook on the household setup and eat what you make.

Northern mountain cooking is its own thing and not what you get in Hanoi or Saigon. It leans on what survives a cold winter at altitude: smoked and dried meat hung above the hearth, fermented greens, and black cardamom, which grows under the forest canopy around Sapa and is one of the area's real export crops rather than a souvenir.

The terraces outside change through the year, flooded and mirroring the sky around May and June, deep green in summer, gold before the September harvest.

This is the booking for a day when cloud sits in the valley, which in Sapa happens often. The class does not depend on a view.

We book with Ethnic Community Cultural Tours directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers the cooking class, guidance from a local host and the preparation of two Vietnamese dishes.

Two hours. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Cooked in a Ta Van home, not a Sapa town kitchen
Two dishes done properly rather than six rushed
Northern mountain food: smoked meat, fermented greens
Black cardamom, grown under the canopy and exported from here
Runs on the cloudy days when Sapa's views close in

fullDescription:
Two hours on spring rolls in Sapa, which are harder to get right than they look.

Vietnamese rolls split into two things people confuse. Fresh rolls, goi cuon, are rolled in softened rice paper and not cooked. Fried rolls, nem ran in the north, are rolled tighter in a thinner wrapper and go into hot oil. The class is about the rolling, because the fillings are forgiving and the wrapping is not.

Rice paper is the thing that catches everyone. It softens in seconds and keeps softening on the board, so you have a narrow window: too dry and it cracks, too wet and it tears as you pull it closed. The fix is working faster than feels comfortable and keeping the fillings drier than you think they should be.

Fillings here follow what the north has: vermicelli, leafy greens, minced pork, wood ear and other mushrooms, herbs from the garden.

You eat what you roll.

The class is indoors in Sapa. Cloud fills this valley for much of the year and closes the views and the flights; this runs regardless, which makes it a sensible thing to hold in reserve for a grey day.

We book with Saigonese Trekking House directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers the class, all ingredients and the rolls you make.

Two hours. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Fresh goi cuon and fried nem ran are two different techniques
Rice paper gives you seconds: too dry cracks, too wet tears
Keep the filling drier than feels right, and work fast
Northern fillings: vermicelli, wood ear, pork, garden herbs
Indoors, so it holds a grey Sapa day together
